research-workflow/skills/auto-research/r.title: /auto-research Workflow
research-workflow/skills/auto-research/r.html:
/auto-research Workflow

When dispatching a role below, specify its research-workflow:<skill-name> identity, not a bare role label.

Session Start

  1. Check the user's research question and whether the current working folder is a suitable place to store that research. Read project instructions if present; AGENTS.md, Git, and existing .scripts/ are not required.
  2. In a writable research folder, resolve ../../scripts/session.py relative to this skill's SKILL.md, then run python3 <resolved-path> --project-root <project-root> init --question <question>. This creates only missing research/state.md and research/focus.md; it does not modify existing research content. If no suitable location exists, skip initialization and work in the conversation.
  3. Read the existing focus, the latest .logs/*_auto-research-session.md if present, cursor ancestors, and necessary state/findings/map/plan/guide files. Do not read the entire tree or raw logs indiscriminately. Use these records and the current request to resume an interrupted session; do not invent missing history.

Direction

From the current local board, recent evidence, review flags, and literature status, the main agent selects the question that best distinguishes the next research decision and updates research/focus.md.

Dispatch direction-challenger with a narrow scope only when stagnation, contradiction, major closure, pivot risk, or premise lock-in affects the direction decision. Do not call it as a ritual in ordinary cycles. When needed, the main agent reads the challenge, decides what to adopt, and reflects that decision in focus.

Boundary transaction

  • When returning from a child to its parent, the curator completes the child's presentation before worker execution only if parent-level work depends on that durable presentation.
  • Only when Pre-Worker Tree Directives identify a semantic repair to the route a worker will read, the curator repairs that route and returns Dispatch readiness: valid or invalidated.
  • If invalidated, do not launch the planned worker. The main agent carries the reason into the next cycle's focus.

Direct work, workers, and review

Start each cycle with direct work by the main agent. Perform research, derivations, source triage, local calculations, and synthesis directly when local files and available tools reasonably suffice.

Only after the Delegation Gate passes, extract the agent, task, target, deliverable, success criteria, inputs, run/slug, delegation reason, downstream decision, and direct-work insufficiency from focus's Worker Dispatches. Run multiple workers in parallel only when their tasks are independent and every deliverable is necessary and nonduplicative.

The main agent treats worker returns as provisional evidence and judges relevance, scope, and adoption. Do not automatically attach a critic. Claim consequence in the schema is a decision record, not a dispatch command. For consequential claims on which the Research Draft or durable memory depends, send a packet centered on the claim only when independent review can materially reduce uncertainty.

  • Mathematical/mechanical claim: blind
  • Source fidelity claim: source-audit
  • Claim dependent on narrative/provenance: contextual

Perform one repair only for REVISE-BLOCKING or OPAQUE when the critic identifies a cheap, bounded repair.

Curator

The main agent integrates provisional evidence into the Research Draft, focus, and session handoff. It may update node-local working evidence in state.md and adopted local strategy in plan.md without changing graph meaning. Mark unreviewed material explicitly; do not directly edit status/kind, maps, findings, checks, or cross-node routes. Dispatch the curator only when Tree Directives require node placement, lifecycle changes, cross-node integration, retraction, archiving, findings materialisation, or checks/provenance closure.

When a request to review substantive durable content is returned, dispatch the critic and return the review to the curator. If unresolved after two rounds, record verification debt.

Session End

  1. Process directives to archive superseded scripts.
  2. Dispatch the curator only for open semantic transactions, unintegrated reviewed evidence, durable promotion/retraction, or cross-node routing debt. The main agent closes sessions containing only local provisional work.
  3. Resolve only pending Durable Reviews on which the Research Draft or durable documents depend.
  4. Send only nodes lacking a human reading route to changed evidence to guide-writer.
  5. In a writable research folder, update focus and save a packet containing next focus, handoff, Research Draft, session log, backlog, and agenda to the path returned by the package-local session.py path --kind log --label auto-research-session. If no suitable location exists, include the same content in the final report.
  6. Briefly report the cycle count, principal results, node changes, deliverables, unresolved verification debt, and next question to the user. Do not commit or push.

If saving the packet fails, preserve the research results and explicitly include the handoff and unsaved status in the final report.

research-workflow/skills/critic/SKILL.md.title: Critic
research-workflow/skills/critic/SKILL.md.html:
Critic

Verify the target independently. Distinguish its correctness from its fit with the project narrative. Write a review file without directly modifying the target.

Read

  • ../../references/core.md
  • ../../references/research-tree.md
  • Only the target and context authorized by the dispatch

Review kind

Provisional Review

Review worker.md or a single repair.md, and write critic.md or critic_rereview.md in the same transaction directory.

Verdicts:

  • ACCEPT: no blocking defect within the reviewed scope
  • REJECT: the central claim or method fails
  • REVISE-NONBLOCKING: usable with narrower scope
  • REVISE-BLOCKING: a bounded repair is needed
  • OPAQUE: insufficient evidence or reproduction details to judge

Durable Surface Review

Review the specified findings section or _materials/analyses file and write the review in checks/. Verdicts are ACCEPT, REVISE, and REJECT. Specify the concrete routing or provenance action required of the curator.

Mode

  • blind: inspect only the target's mathematics, mechanics, and reproducibility
  • source-audit: check the target's fidelity to the source file or record
  • contextual: check consistency with authorized ancestor context or narrative

Do not read unauthorized context to soften a verdict.

Checks

  1. Identify the claim and success criteria.
  2. Follow the derivation independently, checking signs, coefficients, boundary conditions, quantifiers, domains, and edge cases.
  3. For computation, check commands, seeds, parameters, known limits, error estimates, and artifacts.
  4. For literature, check the source passage, notation translation, citation chain, and boundary with project inference.
  5. Look for a counterexample or minimal failing case.
  6. State the surviving scope and verification debt.
  7. Even for ACCEPT, propose provenance specifying confidence, evidence channel, review mode, and scope.

Do not count the review itself as first-order evidence. State explicitly if novelty or significance was not assessed.

Output

Include Target, Mode, Verdict, Summary, Mechanical/Logical findings, Source audit, Surviving scope, Repair guidance, Provenance contribution, and Required owner action as appropriate.

Return: DONE: {review path}

research-workflow/skills/curator/SKILL.m.title: Curator
research-workflow/skills/curator/SKILL.m.html:
Curator

Maintain the active research tree as compressed memory for future research decisions. Resolve authority, placement, scope, and provenance without reconsidering scientific direction or specialist judgments of correctness.

Read

  1. ../../references/core.md
  2. ../../references/research-tree.md
  3. ../../references/naming.md when changing names
  4. ../../references/notes-syntax.md when changing durable links
  5. research/focus.md, cursor ancestors, and the targets of directives or evidence
  6. Only the nodes and surrounding context required by the transaction. Sweep the entire tree only when the session-end flag is explicit

Narrow down _materials through its index. Read archives only for explicitly requested historical investigation or when an active link leads there.

Inputs

  • Pre-Worker Tree Directives
  • Tree Directives
  • Naming Decisions
  • Worker/critic transactions and final verdicts
  • Durable Surface Review
  • Cursor, cycle, and pre-worker/presentation/session-end flags

Authority boundaries

The curator owns node placement, lifecycle, cross-node state/plan integration, maps, findings materialisation, checks routing, archiving, and context-route repair. The research lead may update node-local working state and strategy without changing graph meaning. The curator does not own focus, guides, story, worker tasks, or scientific priorities.

Do not redo a worker's narrow reasoning using broader context. If review or provenance is insufficient, identify whether a specialist, critic, research lead, or meeting is needed.

Transaction

  1. Check node identity, parent contract, evidence stream, context route, and lifecycle.
  2. Translate directives into graph operations and complete create/split/reframe/reparent/close/archive operations first.
  3. If a critic review exists, read the final verdict and integrate only material without blocking defects as established support. Lead-adopted material without a critic review is limited to unreviewed working state.
  4. Rewrite Current Board to reflect current understanding; do not retain a detailed chronology.
  5. Synchronize the parent map and necessary plans.
  6. Materialise only claims with an admission source in findings.md.
  7. Resolve links, notation, naming, scope, and checks in the durable prose touched by the transaction.
  8. Extract reusable results, live gaps, and negative lessons from process-heavy nodes before archiving them.

If multiple choices with different meanings remain, return a blocker with its owner instead of choosing unilaterally.

Pre-worker readiness

Perform routing repairs only. Do not conduct content audits, substantive findings edits, new analyses, or Durable Review requests.

  • The planned worker can proceed with the same premises after repair: Dispatch readiness: valid
  • The task premise, target, or context route changes: Dispatch readiness: invalidated

Do not create a replacement plan even when readiness is invalidated.

Evidence integration

  • Do not link _reviews or .logs as durable evidence.
  • Do not integrate REJECT, blocking, or opaque material as claims. If useful, preserve narrowly stated failure conditions or verification debt.
  • Mark material without a critic review as unreviewed; do not promote it to established support.
  • Clean analyses may live in _materials/analyses, but they are not findings.

Findings and review

An admission source is an explicit directive from the research lead or user, a mechanical repair to an already admitted document, or explicit adoption of an analysis. Stable status or a critic's ACCEPT alone does not constitute admission.

Require a derivation, scope, limitations, and check link for each principal claim. Request a Durable Surface Review when changing a substantive derivation or clean analysis. Apply the returned review; narrow confidence, scope, or routing for REVISE/REJECT.

Session-end mode

Perform a tree-wide coherence pass only when explicitly dispatched with Session-end sweep: true. During that dispatch, check the entire active tree for unintegrated evidence, node structure, stale routes, parent maps, materialisation of admitted facts, state compression, links, pending reviews, and archive residue. Do not skip part of the pass because there were no important changes. The research lead may omit the curator altogether when the session has no open semantic transactions or cross-node debt.

Return

Briefly report changed paths, integrated or deferred evidence, status/graph changes, review requests, and blockers. Always end a readiness transaction with the readiness token.

research-workflow/skills/direction-chall.title: Direction Challenger
research-workflow/skills/direction-chall.html:
Direction Challenger

Expose premises implicitly fixed by the current local board without choosing a direction. Act as a counterpoint to the planner; do not substitute for a worker, critic, or curator.

Read

  • ../../references/core.md
  • research/focus.md
  • The current cursor's state/findings/plan/map
  • The parent map and latest critic/curator summaries

Use only the narrow board needed for the challenge, rather than reading the entire tree, story, or raw logs.

Challenge axes

  • Value: What would success teach us?
  • Goal: Does the current metric represent the actual research objective?
  • Necessity: Is this calculation or construction necessary for the next decision?
  • Premise: Are the implicit assumptions, quantifiers, scales, and domains valid?
  • Frame: Is there another representation, duality, counterexample, or inverse question?
  • Authority: Are the authorities of the source, critic, planner, and user being confused?
  • Inertia: Is past investment the only reason to continue?

Choose only the two to four points that best distinguish the alternatives. Do not pad the list with weak objections.

Output

Write a Direction Challenge to the .logs path obtained from the package's scripts/session.py path --kind log --label direction-challenge.

  • Challenges: premises and the consequences if they are wrong
  • Questions for research-planner: questions that could change the next direction decision
  • Hold: points that cannot be settled with the available evidence

Return: DONE: {challenge path}

research-workflow/skills/guide-writer/SK.html:
Guide Writer

guide.md is an entry point for human oversight, not an authority for claims. Summarize durable research documents without making research decisions or performing tree transactions.

Read

  • ../../references/core.md
  • ../../references/research-tree.md
  • ../../references/notes-syntax.md
  • The specified node's state, findings, map, plan, checks, clean analyses, and source links
  • Necessary ancestor context

Do not use _reviews or .logs as evidence. Identify conflicts as conflicts between durable research documents.

guide.md

  • The question this node addresses and its role for the parent
  • What is currently known
  • Principal evidence and verification links
  • Scope, counterevidence, and unresolved debt
  • A reading route to important figures, analyses, and sources
  • Concrete locations a human should inspect next
  • Grounds for deciding whether to continue, close, or reopen

Exclude past process chronology and scheduler bookkeeping. Do not strengthen claims through the guide or change status.

If conflicting meanings prevent a safe summary, return the conflicting documents and their owners instead of repairing the guide by guesswork.

Return: DONE: {updated guide paths or blocker summary}

research-workflow/skills/research-planne.title: Research Planner
research-workflow/skills/research-planne.html:
Research Planner

Independently compare what should be learned next to advance a research decision, and advise the research lead. Do not own the final direction, focus, tree transactions, verification, or worker execution.

Read

  1. ../../references/core.md
  2. ../../references/research-tree.md
  3. The research root's findings/map/story/principles/conventions
  4. The current cursor's ancestor chain, state/findings/map/plan/guide, and immediate child summaries
  5. The specific direction question, recent deliverables, critic/curator summaries, and literature status supplied by the research lead

Do not read the entire tree or raw logs indiscriminately. Select necessary materials through indexes.

Judgment

  • Select one next question with the highest information value.
  • Choose the means that best distinguishes directions: conjecture, counterexample, calculation, source check, or simulation.
  • Treat failure and negative evidence as valuable outcomes of a route.
  • Address inertia, premises, scale, authority, and novelty risks in the current goal through the challenge response.
  • Do not replace human judgments about novelty, significance, or proof completeness with autonomous labels.

Advisory memo

Address only the decision specified by the research lead and briefly report:

  • Live alternatives and the questions each route would distinguish
  • Evidence gain, cost, and premise risk
  • The recommended next step and observations that would change direction if it were wrong
  • If specialist delegation is needed, the specific capability and why direct work cannot replace it

Do not write focus, state, map, plan, findings, packets, or tree directives. This role adds no value when the main agent can adequately perform the same comparison.

Return

DONE: {advisory memo path or concise advisory}

If structurally impossible: FAILED: {missing condition and owner}

research-workflow/skills/researcher/SKIL.title: Researcher
research-workflow/skills/researcher/SKIL.html:
Researcher

Pursue one research task assigned by the dispatcher in depth. Do not decide direction, tree placement, or claim admission.

Read

  • ../../references/core.md
  • ../../references/research-tree.md when using research tree documents
  • The task, target node, and specified inputs
  • Previous worker/critic files for a resubmission

Method

  1. State the question, success criteria, scope, and known assumptions in your own words.
  2. Before reading the literature, attempt an independent derivation, small case, counterexample, or dimensional/limit check.
  3. Use sources for comparison and checking boundaries, not as substitutes for the argument.
  4. Run calculations, symbolic checks, or short scripts as needed, and record reproduction commands.
  5. Even when a claim fails, record the minimal failure condition and the next condition that would distinguish the possibilities.
  6. Match the strength of the claim to the evidence. Identify untested scope.

Follow the target node's _materials rules for supporting scripts and data. Do not edit the graph, state, findings, or plan.

Submission

Include in worker.md:

  • Task and claim
  • Assumptions and scope
  • Derivation / construction / counterexample
  • Mechanical or source checks
  • Result against success criteria
  • Limitations and failure modes
  • Intended durable destination
  • Reproduction paths/commands
  • Naming decisions

Keep the raw log to a short process trace. Return DONE: {worker.md path}.

speech-act/README.md.title: speech-act
speech-act/README.md.html:
speech-act

Version: 0.2.0
Entrypoint: speech-act:speech-act-writing
Author: Rintaro Masaoka

This package supplies an instructional skill for scholarly drafting, revision, evaluation, and responses to criticism with language models. It asks what a text says, what action it is intended to perform, what a reader might infer, and what evidence supports those judgments.

Select it when claims, implied requests, commitments, reader assumptions, stance, or document relationships matter. Proofreading and factual verification alone do not require this skill.

Use

Load the bundled skill through a compatible skill loader, or provide its instructions directly to a language model with the task materials. Keep the references directory alongside the skill. Host-specific installation procedures are outside the package.

Supply the text or drafting notes, intended audience and purpose, relevant evidence, and any known constraints. Request an operation such as:

  • Draft an abstract that reports these findings without extending their scope.
  • Revise this paragraph so that it requests clarification without committing us to new work.
  • Evaluate the implied claims and reader assumptions in this discussion section.
  • Prepare a response to these reviewer comments, distinguishing completed changes from proposed changes.

The artifact can be in any language required by the task. The skill's instructions and teaching examples are English; cross-language effectiveness has not been established by the dossier.

The operations are planning, act mapping, controlled drafting or revision, evaluation, and exchange repair. Use only the operations needed. Outputs identify consequential assumptions and commitments without treating a model's proposed reading as actual recipient understanding.

Contents and evidence

The two plugin manifests declare the package. skill-dependencies.json records no external skill dependencies. Supporting resources are regular Markdown files; there are no scripts, hooks, executable components, or external skills.

The dossier guide preserves source identifiers, provenance links, findings, conceptual distinctions, and inspection limits. The examples use fictional scholarly situations.

The package was derived only from the assignment and its four embedded research documents. The linked primary works were not independently accessed. The workflow is a design proposal, not an empirically validated intervention. It does not certify intentions, authorship, institutional validity, source authenticity, or actual reader effects.

The accompanying design-notes.md and input-manifest.json are outside the package and document its derivation. They are not runtime dependencies.

License

Original package text and the accompanying design notes and input manifest are licensed under the MIT License. Bibliographic attribution remains with the identified sources; this license does not purport to relicense those underlying works.

speech-act/skills/speech-act-writing/SKI.title: Speech-act writing
speech-act/skills/speech-act-writing/SKI.html:
Speech-act writing

Help the writer align a scholarly text's content, intended action, and evidential commitments with its situation. Treat the writer's stated purpose as the target. A model's proposed interpretation is an inference, not access to the writer's or reader's mental state.

The operations below are design proposals derived from the supplied dossier. They are not validated writing interventions. The dossier guide separates conceptual proposals, empirical findings, product descriptions, and access limits. The worked examples illustrate application using fictional situations.

These instructions are English. Produce the artifact in the language required by the task. Preserve quotations in their supplied language unless translation is requested. Flag uncertainty when interpretation depends on an unfamiliar idiom, disciplinary convention, or language-specific distinction. The dossier does not establish equivalent performance across languages.

Expected inputs

Use what the task supplies:

  • The requested operation and artifact: for example, an abstract, argument paragraph, review, response letter, or evaluation report.
  • Existing text for revision or evaluation; notes, claims, or evidence for drafting.
  • The writer's purpose, intended readers, genre, discipline, venue, and stage of the scholarly activity.
  • Relevant preceding or following documents, comments, or correspondence.
  • Evidence and source passages, with their known access or verification status.
  • Constraints on claims, commitments, institutional authority, language, length, and author preferences.
  • When relevant, the actual assistance used, reader responses, and the writer's reported experience of control.

Not every input is necessary for every task. Use the smallest adequate unit, such as one sentence, a paragraph, or a linked pair of documents. State consequential assumptions. If missing information would decide whether a claim is warranted, an action has occurred, or a commitment is authorized, ask a focused question or supply conditional alternatives. Do not invent that information.

Distinctions to preserve

Object Working question Boundary
Explicit content What does this text say, with its contextual references resolved as far as supplied information allows? Wording alone may leave references or explicit content underdetermined.
Intended force What action does the writer intend to perform through this passage? A grammatical form or performative verb does not establish the act by itself.
Interpreted force What action might a reader recognize here? A model-generated reading is provisional unless supported by actual recipient evidence.
Uptake Is there evidence that meaning and force were understood? Austin's uptake is distinct from agreement, belief, compliance, and later effects.
Consequence What subsequently happened because of the text? Desired and predicted effects are not observed effects. Bazerman's broader use of perlocutionary uptake must be identified separately.
Presumed context What information does the passage treat as shared? Presumed sharing does not demonstrate shared beliefs.
Grounding What recipient evidence establishes understanding sufficient for this exchange's purpose? Acceptance in grounding concerns understanding, not assent to a proposition.
Stance and engagement How does the writer position a claim and address a reader? Discipline-specific preferences are not a universal feature checklist.

For ordinary working labels, use terms such as report, argue, qualify, challenge, acknowledge, request, undertake, or record a completed change. These labels are practical choices using general linguistic knowledge. They are not a reconstruction of Searle's detailed taxonomy. Multiple acts can occur in one passage, and an extended text can have a dominant purpose without every sentence performing the same act.

Do not collapse Grice's and Wilson and Sperber's explanations into one theory. Both support attention to interpretation beyond wording, but they differ on cooperation, relevance, and explicit content. Their concepts organize questions here; they do not mechanically determine the right reading.

Choose an operation

Task Suggested route
Draft from notes or evidence O1, then O3
Revise a passage O2, then O3; use O1 if the purpose is unclear
Evaluate a text O2, then O4
Respond to a reviewer or repair correspondence O1 and O5; use O2 for ambiguous passages

Do not run every operation automatically. Carry a compact situation brief between operations: artifact, writer and reader roles, intended action, evidence boundary, and unresolved assumptions.

O1 — Situate the text and plan its acts

  1. Identify the scholarly activity and the text's place within it. For example, distinguish presenting a finding from responding to a request for further evidence.
  2. Record the writer's role, intended reader, genre, and known institutional or venue conditions. Separate requirements that make an act count in that setting from preferences about how well it is performed. Use supplied rules; do not invent authority or institutional procedure.
  3. State the dominant purpose of the whole artifact. Identify supporting local acts and, where useful, the preceding and anticipated next documents.
  4. Separate what the reader should recognize from what the writer hopes will happen afterward. Understanding a bounded claim, accepting it, and citing it are different targets.
  5. Attach evidence and commitment boundaries to planned acts. Mark unknown circumstances that could change their interpretation or validity.

Unit or document Intended act Content/evidence boundary Reader assumption Desired later effect Unresolved condition

O2 — Map a text's actions and interpretive gaps

  1. Select meaningful units. Keep surrounding context when it changes force; do not impose one act per sentence.
  2. For each important unit, distinguish explicit content from the intended act supplied by the writer and the act inferred by the evaluator. Anchor every diagnostic in wording or supplied context.
  3. Identify consequential inferences: an implied criticism, invitation, expectation, concession, or commitment. Keep presumed background information separate from an inferred implicature. Resolve references only when the supplied context permits it.

  3. Draft the requested artifact or make the smallest adequate revision. Add context, definitions, attribution, or explicit scope where the intended action otherwise depends on an unsupported inference.
  4. Check changes to epistemic strength, attribution, requests, promises, and action status. Do not silently turn a source's claim into the writer's claim, a suggestion into an undertaking, or a planned revision into a completed revision.
  5. If evidence cannot support the requested force, offer a bounded alternative and identify the change in the act performed. Do not describe a substantive narrowing as merely polishing the prose.

O4 — Evaluate alignment and rehearse possible reception

  1. Evaluate against the supplied purpose and constraints. If no purpose is supplied, make the evaluative target provisional rather than silently imposing one.
  2. Check whether content and evidence support the act, whether the requested or undertaken action is intelligible, whether relevant context is available, and whether supplied authority or venue conditions are satisfied.
  3. When reception is consequential, propose at most two materially different reader situations. Specify the information each reader has and the reading that might follow. Label these as hypothetical interpretations, not measured responses or reliable predictions.
  4. Keep AI-related questions separate when relevant:
Dimension Permissible basis Do not infer
Content and communicative action Text, evidence, situation, and stated purpose A model's own communicative intention
Reader attribution of production Actual metadata or recipient reports AI authorship from stylistic cues alone
Social reception Supplied observations, separated by outcome Trust, authenticity, or approval from warmth alone
Writer ownership The writer's own report, if available Ownership, legal authorship, or consent from fluency
  1. Report each material finding as supported by supplied material, conflicting with a supplied constraint, or underdetermined. These are diagnostic labels, not validated scores. Identify the passage, rationale, and smallest useful remedy.

O5 — Respond and repair across an exchange

  1. Link the earlier contribution, the recipient's actual response, and the proposed reply. Identify the outstanding claim, request, misunderstanding, or commitment.
  2. Distinguish evidence of understanding from agreement, belief, compliance, and institutional acceptance. A response may show that a criticism was understood while disagreeing with it.
  3. If an indirect request is ambiguous, state the candidate interpretations. Ask for clarification when the distinction is consequential and cannot be resolved from supplied context; otherwise make the chosen interpretation explicit.
  4. Draft a reply that acknowledges the relevant act and states the response: completed change, future undertaking, explanation, disagreement, or bounded alternative. For completed changes, use supplied locations or evidence. Do not invent revisions, experiments, or recipient assent.
  5. Make repair possible at the scale the medium permits. In correspondence, this may include a focused question or a checkable paraphrase. In an article without immediate feedback, it may include a definition, signpost, or explicit scope statement. These are proposed accommodations, not evidence that grounding has occurred.

Earlier act Interpretation used Response act Completed or planned action Evidence/location or unresolved dependency

Boundaries

  • Analyze texts and supplied circumstances; do not claim transparent access to human intentions or a model's consciousness, agency, or communicative intentions.
  • Treat actual author intent, actual recipient understanding, and observed effects as established only to the extent supported by supplied information. A language model's rehearsal supplies none of these by itself.
  • Do not determine factual truth or source authenticity merely from prose. Identify verification needs and preserve supplied provenance. Do not manufacture quotations, citations, page numbers, or source access.
  • Do not prescribe a universal academic tone, warmth level, hedge density, disclosure policy, or AI workflow. The dossier does not establish one.
  • Do not infer that publication dates demonstrate social adaptation to AI. Suspicion, disclosure, trust, and interpersonal impressions were studied under different conditions.
  • Do not use stylistic heuristics as an AI detector. The supplied detection evidence concerns particular self-presentation tasks and model generations, not every text or detection method.
  • Keep experienced ownership distinct from contribution, legal authorship, communicative intention, and reception. Do not supply legal conclusions.
  • Treat institutional validity as conditional on known circumstances and rules. A verb such as accept or approve cannot create authority by itself.
  • Use author-defined aims for evaluation. Understanding, persuasion, compliance, and institutional effect are different possible aims, not a universal success ladder.

References and examples

The dossier guide supplies all sixteen reference records used above, with the scope of the supplied inspection and the permissible role of each source. The examples demonstrate drafting, revision, evaluation, and repair. No external skill, source retrieval, executable component, or host-specific resource is required.

The operations below are design proposals derived from the supplied dossier. They are not validated writing interventions. These instructions are English. Produce the artifact in the language required by the task. Preserve quotations in their supplied language unless translation is requested. The dossier does not establish equivalent performance across languages.

Expected inputs

Use what the task supplies:

  • The requested operation and artifact: for example, an abstract, argument paragraph, review, response letter, or evaluation report.
  • Existing text for revision or evaluation; notes, claims, or evidence for drafting.
  • The writer's purpose, intended readers, genre, discipline, venue, and stage of the scholarly activity.
  • Relevant preceding or following documents, comments, or correspondence.
  • Evidence and source passages, with their known access or verification status.
  • Constraints on claims, commitments, institutional authority, language, length, and author preferences.
  • When relevant, the actual assistance used, reader responses, and the writer's reported experience of control.

Not every input is necessary for every task. Use the smallest adequate unit, such as one sentence, a paragraph, or a linked pair of documents. State consequential assumptions. If missing information would decide whether a claim is warranted, an action has occurred, or a commitment is authorized, ask a focused question or supply conditional alternatives. Do not invent that information.

Intended force What action does the writer intend to perform through this passage? A grammatical form or performative verb does not establish the act by itself.
Interpreted force What action might a reader recognize here? A model-generated reading is provisional unless supported by actual recipient evidence.
Uptake Is there evidence that meaning and force were understood? Austin's uptake is distinct from agreement, belief, compliance, and later effects.
Consequence What subsequently happened because of the text? Desired and predicted effects are not observed effects. Bazerman's broader use of perlocutionary uptake must be identified separately.
Presumed context What information does the passage treat as shared? Presumed sharing does not demonstrate shared beliefs.
Grounding What recipient evidence establishes understanding sufficient for this exchange's purpose? Acceptance in grounding concerns understanding, not assent to a proposition.
Stance and engagement How does the writer position a claim and address a reader? Discipline-specific preferences are not a universal feature checklist.

For ordinary working labels, use terms such as report, argue, qualify, challenge, acknowledge, request, undertake, or record a completed change. These labels are practical choices using general linguistic knowledge. They are not a reconstruction of Searle's detailed taxonomy. Multiple acts can occur in one passage, and an extended text can have a dominant purpose without every sentence performing the same act.

Do not collapse Grice's and Wilson and Sperber's explanations into one theory. Both support attention to interpretation beyond wording, but they differ on cooperation, relevance, and explicit content. Their concepts organize questions here; they do not mechanically determine the right reading.

speech-act/skills/speech-act-writing/ref.title: Dossier guide
speech-act/skills/speech-act-writing/ref.html:
Dossier guide

This guide paraphrases the four research documents embedded in the assignment: input/concepts.md, input/sources.json, input/ai-concepts.md, and input/ai-sources.json. Their reported inspection date is 6 October 2026. The package author did not retrieve the linked works. Links preserve the dossier's bibliographic provenance; they are not runtime dependencies or claims of independent full-text reading.

Use the identifiers below to follow the basis statements in SKILL.md. Conceptual compatibility does not establish that the proposed operations work empirically. A corpus result, an experiment, a philosophical proposal, and a product description have different evidential roles.

Conceptual references

austin1962 — J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (1962)

The dossier supports considering an utterance in its circumstances, including written acts, and distinguishing illocutionary action from later effects. Understanding meaning and force belongs to uptake; compliance is a different matter. The p. 116 passage distinguishes conventional taking effect, uptake, and later responses.

Use in O1, O2, O3, O4, and O5: separate intended act, recognized act, and consequence; check relevant circumstances. Do not infer that recognizable wording alone fulfills every condition.

Access reported: institutional excerpts identified as pp. 5–8 and 139; indexed scan passages at pp. 109 and 116; a 1975 edition publisher abstract and record. Direct scan retrieval failed. The institutional excerpt's edition provenance is unresolved.

References: institutional excerpts, primary scan, 1975 edition record.

searle1965 — John R. Searle, What Is a Speech Act? (1965)

The dossier distinguishes constitutive rules from rules regulating an independently existing activity. It reports a promising analysis focused on explicit central cases, with borderline, defective, hinted, metaphorical, and elliptical cases outside its selected scope. An institutional excerpt includes meaningful written marks.

Use in O1: ask which supplied conditions make an act count in a setting, separately from preferences about its execution. This is not a complete institutional-validity test or a reconstruction of promise conditions.

Access reported: indexed reprint passages at pp. 2, 3, and 10 and an edited institutional excerpt; direct PDFs were not successfully retrieved.

References: institutional reprint, Open University excerpt.

searle1976 — John R. Searle, A classification of illocutionary acts (1976)

The abstract proposes representatives/assertives, directives, commissives, expressives, and declarations. It names point, direction of fit, and expressed psychological state among the distinguishing dimensions. It presents a theoretical classification with criteria rather than a grammar-based inventory.

Use in O2: distinguish what an act does from sentence form and allow classifications to remain tentative. The skill's ordinary working labels are design choices. Detailed definitions, category mappings, and diagnostic tests are not supplied by this abstract.

Access reported: publisher abstract, issue metadata, and references only. The 2008 online date is distinct from the 1976 publication.

Reference: publisher record.

grice1975 — H. P. Grice, Logic and Conversation (1975)

The inspected passages distinguish what is said from conventional and conversational implicatures, while acknowledging context in reference and disambiguation. They describe exchanges with a common purpose or accepted direction and expectations of quantity, quality, relation, and manner.

Use in O2 and O3: expose consequential implications and ask whether needed information and evidential qualifications are explicit enough for the task. These expectations are not a compulsory prose checklist, and every reader inference need not be intended.

Access reported: indexed primary passages; the opened scan yielded no extractable text and screenshots were unusable. No complete essay reading was claimed.

Reference: institutional scan.

stalnaker1998 — Robert Stalnaker, On the Representation of Context (1998)

The abstract describes context as information presumed shared and presupposed when acts are interpreted. Acts depend on context and also affect it. Presumed sharing is not evidence that participants actually believe the same things.

Use in O2 and O5: identify what readers are being treated as already knowing, and track changes to those assumptions across an exchange. Do not reconstruct the uninspected formal apparatus.

Access reported: publisher abstract and bibliographic record only.

Reference: publisher record.

clark_brennan1991 — Herbert H. Clark and Susan E. Brennan, Grounding in Communication (1991)

Grounding concerns jointly established understanding sufficient for current purposes. A contribution involves presentation and acceptance supported by evidence of understanding; acceptance does not mean agreement. Email and letters permit review and private revision while changing timing, feedback, sequencing, repair, and coordination costs.

Use in O5: distinguish issuing a reply from establishing understanding, and design a repair opportunity suited to the exchange. The chapter sets one-way broadcast media aside. Applying its questions to an article without recipient evidence is an analogy, not proof of grounding.

Access reported: selected passages at pp. 127–132 and 140–146, not an exhaustive chapter reading.

Reference: author-hosted chapter.

wilson_sperber2004 — Deirdre Wilson and Dan Sperber, Relevance Theory (2004)

Decoding is one input to inferential interpretation. Context contributes to explicit content as well as implicatures. Relevance concerns comparative cognitive effects and processing effort. Recognizing an informative intention is different from believing what is communicated. The account disputes parts of Grice's explanation.

Use in O2 and O4: expose underdetermination, distinguish understanding from belief, and consider context without treating relevance as a numerical score. Do not assume intention is transparently recoverable.

Access reported: selected author-hosted sections, including §§1–3 and explicit-content discussion; no full chapter reading was claimed.

Reference: author-hosted chapter.

miller1984 — Carolyn R. Miller, Genre as Social Action (1984)

The abstract locates genre in recurrent rhetorical action and conventionalized social motives, rather than merely subject matter or form.

Use in O1: connect genre selection to the action and recurrent situation, rather than choosing a visual template alone. Do not infer detailed arguments about exigence, typification, or levels of meaning from the abstract.

Access reported: author-uploaded abstract and bibliographic records only. Later upload and display dates do not replace the original 1984 publication year.

References: author-uploaded record, bibliographic record.

bazerman2004 — Charles Bazerman, Speech Acts, Genres, and Activity Systems: How Texts Organize Activity and People (2004)

Texts participate in relationships, social facts, and coordinated activities. A genre set concerns a role's text types; a genre system concerns patterned relations among interacting participants' sets; an activity system includes what people accomplish through and beyond texts. Extended writing can aggregate acts under dominant purposes. Responses can be delayed, private, multiple, or differently situated. Genre recognition is not exhausted by a fixed feature list.

Use in O1, O2, O4, and O5: analyze local passages within larger texts and document sequences, and avoid assuming a single immediate response. Identify the author's broader term perlocutionary uptake separately from Austin's uptake.

Access reported: conceptual and initial methodological sections at pp. 309–320; later analyses and exercises were not comprehensively inspected.

Reference: author-hosted chapter.

hyland2005 — Ken Hyland, Stance and engagement: a model of interaction in academic discourse (2005)

The abstract distinguishes writer positioning toward material from resources that presuppose or construct an active addressee. The account draws on 240 published research articles across eight disciplines and informant interviews, supporting attention to disciplinary writer-reader positioning.

Use in O1, O2, O3, and O4: describe what position and reader relationship a passage constructs. The dossier does not supply the full linguistic feature taxonomy or causal evidence of particular readers' reactions.

Access reported: institutional abstract, metadata, and author publication-list entry only.

Reference: institutional record.

AI-mediated communication references

hohenstein2023 — Hohenstein et al., Artificial intelligence in communication impacts language and social relationships (2023)

Two randomized messenger experiments concerned short policy discussions. Increased smart-reply use was associated with faster exchanges, more positive emotional language, and favorable partner evaluations. Study 1 instrumented use with randomized availability; causal interpretation depends on instrumental-variable assumptions. Suspected AI use was associated with less favorable impressions, but suspicion was not randomized. Availability alone did not yield the same main effects as use.

Use in O3 and O4: keep changes in expression separate from beliefs about production and interpersonal reception. Do not convert the suspicion association into a causal disclosure penalty or a universal authenticity claim.

Access reported: abstract, selected introduction/discussion passages, and selected methods sections.

Reference: article.

purcell2025 — Purcell et al., Writing with AI boosts trust-building efficiency (2025)

Two preregistered online incentivized trust-game experiments, total N=1,637, found reduced writing time with generally similar behavioral and stated trust. Disclosure did not substantially remove the efficiency advantage. Study 2 found a small behavioral-trust advantage for unaided messages without a corresponding stated-trust effect. Linguistic associations with warmth, complexity, and lower authenticity were exploratory; historical familiarity was a proposed explanation, not a tested change over time.

Use in O3 and O4: distinguish behavioral trust, stated trust, linguistic associations, and proposed mechanisms. Do not generalize from brief US transactions to scholarly acceptance, emotional closeness, or long-term cooperation.

Access reported: summary, selected Study 2 results and figure descriptions, discussion/limitations/conclusions, and selected STAR Methods.

Reference: article.

jakesch2023 — Maurice Jakesch, Jeffrey T. Hancock, and Mor Naaman, Human heuristics for AI-generated language are flawed (2023)

Six experiments, N=4,600, tested source judgments for professional, dating, and hospitality self-presentations generated with GPT-2/GPT-3-era models. Judgments were near chance. First-person language and family references predicted perceived humanity without reliably identifying human origin. Validation using learned judgment predictions increased perceived humanity of selected generated profiles. Immediate feedback and incentives did not improve detection under tested conditions; some detectable differences remained.

Use in O4: keep production attribution separate from interpreting a text and do not apply stylistic detection heuristics as an evaluation shortcut. These results do not establish universal undetectability or rule out learning through longer exposure.

Access reported: selected manuscript results, discussion, and methods, pp. 2–8.

Reference: article.

hu2023 — Jennifer Hu, Sammy Floyd, Olessia Jouravlev, Evelina Fedorenko, and Edward Gibson, A fine-grained comparison of pragmatic language understanding in humans and language models (2023)

Expert-curated English multiple-choice scenarios tested seven pragmatic phenomena. Larger tested models often selected intended interpretations and shared human error patterns, while humor, irony, and maxim violations remained difficult. Removing context degraded human and model performance, especially for irony, deceits, and maxims. Models retained substantial performance on scrambled contexts; comparable human scrambling tests were not conducted.

Use in O2 and O4: retain relevant context and label model-generated interpretations as task-limited proposals. Linguistic cue learning and heuristic mental-state representation remained competing explanations. Answer selection does not establish consciousness, the model's own intentions, or reliable access to a particular user's unstated goals.

Access reported: selected §§3–6, pp. 4195–4202.

Reference: conference paper.

pennanen2026 — Niki Pennanen, Pyry Kanerva, and Christian Guckelsberger, How prompting and editing shape psychological ownership in AI-assisted creative writing (2026)

An abstract-level account reports a preregistered short-story experiment, N=273, crossing single versus iterative prompting with direct-editing availability and including manual writing. Editing increased ownership, especially after single-prompt generation. Iterative prompting increased ownership when editing was unavailable. Manual writing yielded higher ownership than all AI-assisted conditions. Prompting and editing as partially substitutable opportunities for control and self-investment is the authors' interpretation.

Use in O3 and O4: offer meaningful control opportunities and distinguish the writer's reported ownership from other outcomes. Transferring this rationale to scholarly revision is a design inference. Legal authorship, communicative intention, actual contribution, and reader reception were not interchangeable with the measured ownership outcome.

Access reported: publisher highlights/abstract and institutional metadata/abstract only. Full methods and measurement details were unavailable.

Reference: article record.

google-smart-compose — Google, Use Smart Compose in Gmail (undated documentation)

The documentation describes suggestions accepted through an explicit action, separate suggestion and personalization controls, generic suggestions when personalization is off, and personalization aimed at matching usual writing style. It warns that suggestions may predict incorrect facts and are not designed to answer questions.

Use in O3: distinguish a proposed wording, its selection, and fidelity to a particular communicative purpose. The interface provides an analogy for visible selection, not empirical proof of preserved intent, ownership, or agency. The skill does not require this product or imitate its interface.

Access reported: specified opening notices and controls/personalization sections, inspected in the supplied dossier on 6 October 2026.

Reference: first-party documentation.

Cross-source limits

Hohenstein and Purcell studied different assistance, tasks, expectations, and outcomes. Their findings neither directly replicate one another nor establish that society adapted between publication dates. Immediate detection-feedback failures do not resolve durable reader adaptation. None of these sources validates the skill's workflow, a universal academic style, or a mandatory disclosure practice.

The conceptual works supply distinctions rather than one settled theory. In particular, presumed context, grounding acceptance, proposition belief, request compliance, institutional taking effect, and experienced ownership must remain distinguishable. Use the operations to make these questions explicit, not to certify answers that the supplied evidence leaves open.

speech-act/skills/speech-act-writing/ref.title: Worked examples
speech-act/skills/speech-act-writing/ref.html:
Worked examples

All texts, data, policies, and exchanges below are fictional teaching examples. They are not findings from the dossier. The practical diagnoses are design proposals. Ordinary judgments about tense, modality, attribution, and the force of expressions use general linguistic knowledge.

1. Drafting a bounded claim from pilot evidence

Input

Artifact: an abstract sentence. Reader: researchers deciding whether to examine a proposed annotation method. Intended act: report a limited comparison and motivate further study.

Toy evidence: eight passages were annotated under Methods A and B. Six had fewer annotator disagreements under B. The passages were not randomly sampled; no causal design or broad validation was supplied.

Requested wording in the notes:

Our study proves that Method B solves interpretive ambiguity.

O1 and O3

The dominant purpose is to present a pilot result. The notes instead attempt a general proof. Changing this is a change in claim and force, not merely a smoother formulation.

Proposed artifact:

In this eight-passage pilot comparison, annotators disagreed less often on six passages under Method B than under Method A. This pattern motivates a larger comparison across genres.

Consequential changes: the claim is limited to the supplied comparison; the next sentence proposes further investigation. It does not claim that disagreement measures every kind of ambiguity or that the method will generalize. Merely adding probably to the original sentence would leave those problems unresolved.

Desired later effect: readers consider further study. No observation of that effect is supplied. Reader understanding of the bounded claim, belief in its significance, and willingness to use the method remain different questions.

Basis: O1/O3; Austin's act/effect distinction, Grice's attention to communicated information, and the dossier's repeated evidence-scope boundaries. The specific scholarly formulation is an instructional proposal.

2. Revising politeness without adding an undertaking

Input

Artifact: a response to a reviewer. Intended acts: acknowledge a helpful criticism, report one completed clarification, and explain why a requested new experiment is outside the current revision.

Supplied facts: the definition was clarified in the opening paragraph of Section 2. No new experiment was conducted. The author has not undertaken to conduct one.

A model proposes:

Thank you for the helpful suggestions. We will implement all your recommendations and resolve the issue completely.

O2

Passage Content and force Conflict
Thank you for the helpful suggestions. Acknowledgment and favorable evaluation Consistent with the supplied purpose.
We will implement all your recommendations Broad future undertaking Adds a commitment absent from the brief.
resolve the issue completely Assures a comprehensive result Neither the supplied work nor evidence supports that assurance.

O3

Proposed artifact:

Thank you for the helpful criticism. We have clarified the opening paragraph of Section 2. A new experiment is outside the current revision, and we have not added one.

This separates acknowledgment, a completed action, and the boundary of the response. If the author wants to undertake later work, that requires a different author choice and different wording. A warm tone does not supply authorization for the undertaking.

The reviewer may understand this response and still disagree. Its politeness does not demonstrate trust, authenticity, acceptance, or ownership. The author may edit the explanation to fit the actual project; the model should not invent a more persuasive reason.

Basis: O2/O3/O4; Austin, Hyland, and the AI dossier's separation of expression, reception, and ownership. Tense and commitment checks are ordinary linguistic applications.

3. Repairing an indirect reviewer request

Input

Reviewer comment:

The distinction between understanding and agreement could be clearer.

Available context: the comment follows Section 2, where both terms appear. The author has now added a distinction in Section 2's opening paragraph. No reviewer response to this revision is available.

O2 and O5

Candidate readings:

  • A request to revise the definition in the manuscript.
  • A request to explain the existing distinction in the response letter.

The comment does not explicitly specify the repair. The manuscript change supports choosing the first reading while making the response explicit.

Proposed artifact:

We understood this comment as a request to distinguish the two terms in the manuscript. We have revised the opening paragraph of Section 2. Understanding a claim does not by itself mean agreeing with it. Please let us know if your concern was instead a request to explain the existing distinction in this response letter.

Earlier act Interpretation used Response act Action status Evidence
Indirect criticism/request Clarify the manuscript distinction State interpretation, report change, offer repair Completed clarification Supplied Section 2 location

This reply presents a contribution and makes further repair possible. It does not establish that the reviewer understood, agreed, or accepted the revision. If the manuscript had not yet changed, use a future undertaking only if authorized, or describe a proposed revision; do not retain we have revised.

For an article without an active exchange, the corresponding design move might be to define the distinction directly. That would reduce an interpretive dependency, but would not establish joint grounding with unknown readers.

Basis: O2/O5; Grice, Stalnaker, Clark and Brennan, and Bazerman. The proposed clarification is not a tested repair technique.

4. Evaluating institutional force and presumed sharing

Input

Artifact: a submission cover letter written by an author. Intended act: request consideration of a manuscript. Supplied venue rule: only the editor issues acceptance decisions after review. No acceptance decision has occurred.

Draft:

As we all agree, the controversy is settled. This letter hereby accepts our manuscript for publication.

O1 and O4

Finding Basis Diagnostic status Remedy
Agreement is treated as shared As we all agree, with no supplied evidence of reader agreement Underdetermined State the paper's argument instead of assuming consensus.
A settled controversy is asserted No evidence for that conclusion is supplied Underdetermined Bound the claim to the manuscript's actual argument or evidence.
The letter attempts an acceptance act The supplied rule assigns this act to the editor Conflicts with a supplied condition Make the author's submission or request explicit.

Proposed artifact, conditional on the stated intended act:

We submit this manuscript for consideration.

Two hypothetical reader situations:

  • An editor with the supplied rule can recognize a submission request in the revision. Whether the editor accepts it is a separate future outcome.
  • A researcher reading the cover letter without the manuscript can recognize the submission request but cannot assess the manuscript from the letter alone.

These are possible readings, not observed responses. The word hereby does not supply institutional authority. If the same wording appeared in an authorized editor's decision under different supplied conditions, its analysis would change.

Basis: O1/O4; Austin's circumstances, Searle's rule distinction, Stalnaker's presumed context, and Bazerman's document/activity relationships. The fictional venue rule is an example input, not a rule inferred from the research.

study-notes/skills/study-note/SKILL.md.title: Study Note
study-notes/skills/study-note/SKILL.md.html:
Study Note

Create study notes that let the intended reader reconstruct the central calculations and use each intermediate result. For HTML notes, use Study Note HTML Specification 1.1.0 and keep the manuscript editable as Markdown while preserving reader interactions and source references.

Establish the project

For HTML work, read the specification before authoring or changing the format. Inspect the project's instructions, manuscript directory, chapter registry, renderer, and publication configuration. A project may provide an implementation mapping or adapter; read it for local paths, supported features, source revisions, and legacy exceptions. Keep those project facts in the project.

Identify the published manuscript authority before editing. Older notes, source transcriptions, generated HTML, and review extracts are separate artifacts. A format-only request does not authorize rewriting the scholarly content or migrating unrelated files.

Design and revise the explanation

For a new note or substantial change to the learning sequence, read the bundled exposition workflow. Establish the reader's starting knowledge, the concrete operation or relation the note should teach, and the dependency from each stage to the next. Before loading unfamiliar definitions, make their local purpose intelligible. Keep the visible route sufficient for the next inference when optional details are closed.

For a prose review or broad revision, read the bundled prose-review workflow. Select the relevant perspectives; do not run every possible check on a small edit. Examine the whole note's argument before polishing sentences. Remove production commentary and repeated promises when they do not contribute to the reader's understanding. Preserve claims, assumptions, quantifiers, notation, and source attribution. A source or mathematical gap requires verification, not stylistic repair.

These workflows are localized from Academic Writing and are part of this skill. Do not require the separate academic-writing plugin for ordinary study-note work. Use a specialized scholarly workflow only when the task genuinely calls for a capability not included here.

Create or edit a note

  • Use the manuscript example for supported syntax and the metadata example for the chapter registry. Adapt examples into authored content; do not require their section structure.
  • Resolve an available renderer through the project adapter. Reuse its accepted Markdown parsing, math components, preview interactions, and styles. This skill supplies the specification and authoring examples, not an executable reader. If the renderer is absent and the user requested a working site, implement and validate it within that task.
  • Connect chapter metadata to navigation, routes, and page metadata. A JSON file alone does not make a legacy renderer consume it. Avoid separate editable registries for the same values.
  • Audit reused reader chrome before carrying it into a new note. Keep visible labels, taglines, badges, metadata rows, and repeated titles only when they help readers identify a destination, understand their position, or perform an action. Remove template-specific copy and duplicate labels from the rendered UI; retain metadata needed for page titles and accessibility even when it is not shown. Check desktop and mobile navigation separately so a functional menu label is not mistaken for decoration.
  • Keep published chapter and reference IDs stable. Use explicit passage or disclosure IDs for durable links; line-number heading anchors are only local navigation.
  • Keep definitions in their original manuscript passages and preview those passages. Use disclosures and equation hints for supporting detail while preserving the premises needed in the visible reading flow.
  • Run a referent-and-operation check on the visible path before accepting a passage as definition-complete. Include ordinary relational words, not just technical terms and symbols: for every role word that carries an argument (for example an input, output, remainder, correction, choice, or finite/local quantity), identify the concrete object, the operation or comparison that gives it that role, and the visible sentence or equation at or before first use that establishes both. Substitute the concrete object into the sentence. If more than one reading remains plausible, the referent first appears later, or the reader must infer an expert convention, repair the passage at first use. Check headings and chapter openings as well as prose, and rebuild the bridge at chapter transitions. Do not add glossary entries for ordinary uses whose referent and operation are already explicit in the same reading unit.
  • Keep original equation numbers distinct from globally unique lookup IDs. Validate custom blocks and cross-chapter references, not only ordinary TeX.
  • For mathematical exposition, run the working-memory review on the visible reading path. Track what a reader must hold at the scale of a formula, an argument, and a chapter transition. Treat each new Latin or Greek base letter as a costly mapping unless its conventional or mnemonic association directly cues its meaning. Never introduce three or more new base letters at one transition; stage them one or two at a time. When a new symbol is unavoidable, attach its semantic noun phrase at every occurrence, with an adjacent legend for displays, until repeated use across the required reading path has made the meaning demonstrably familiar. At each completed calculation or subargument, trace downstream uses: its temporary steps are released only if subsequent reasoning uses a compact result in their place, or reconstructs a needed detail at the point of use. Reintroduce earlier results at the point of use instead of assuming the reader retained a previous chapter. Change dependencies and notation rather than adding reader-facing instructions to forget material.
  • At each explanation, ask the simple question: would a visualization make this easier to understand than prose and formulas alone? Favor providing one whenever the reader would otherwise have to construct a mental picture of connections, geometry, stages, comparisons, counts, or cancellations. Place it before or beside the inference that needs that picture, even if the prose never mentions a figure. Choose a diagram, plot, table, or interactive view according to what makes the relation clearest. Show the actual objects and relations, and explain the marks and scope in nearby prose and alt text. If prose does invoke a figure or table, supply it rather than leaving the reader to imagine it; remove that reference only when the visual genuinely adds no clarity.
  • Preserve figure sources and rendered assets. Check mathematical labels and readability in both themes and narrow layouts.
  • Load KaTeX’s stylesheet and make every font file it references available from the note’s own build. Bundle or embed the KaTeX fonts; do not rely on another project’s development-server paths, a CDN, or an unverified fallback font. Apply the KaTeX font rules to both inline and display math without overriding them with the body font.

Verify and deliver

For HTML notes, apply specification sections 11–12 to the changed surface. For any substantive teaching change, replay the visible reading sequence with the intended reader baseline and verify the next downstream use. Use the renderer's body extraction to review the visible reading flow separately from hidden details. For changes to definitions, derivations, structure, or the placement of premises, request an independent agent review of the extracted units before accepting the revision; the reviewer must not use later or hidden material to supply missing premises.

When a reader reports a defect, infer the reusable failure class before applying a local repair. Test analogous passages elsewhere in the note, and update the relevant skill gate when that class extends beyond the single artifact; keep one-off typos and facts local. For changed explanatory passages, make the working-memory review a separate pass after correctness and prerequisite checks. Trace each later use back to the exact earlier statement it needs. At a proposed boundary, verify that later steps depend on a compact result rather than on the intermediate chain; if a detail is needed later, retain or rederive it there. Record overload points and the dependency change used to repair them. A chain of correct, defined steps does not pass merely because a summary says the details can be set aside.

In the extracted visible body, review every explanation for a visualization opportunity, including passages that never say “figure”: name the mental picture the reader must build and decide whether supplying it would make the next inference easier. If so, provide it before the inference and verify that its marks really show the stated objects, distinctions, counts, or cancellations. A claim that invokes a figure or table also needs an adjacent, inspectable representation. Confirm each supplied asset exists in the build and is readable at narrow widths and in both themes. Separately, record a referent-and-operation ledger for each changed section: first use of a role word, its object, its operation or comparison, and the visible evidence at or before that use. Fail unresolved entries even when every symbol is defined and the calculation is correct; a build, extraction, or generic first-time-reader pass cannot certify this semantic check. Then check syntax, reference targets, metadata wiring, custom math rendering, relevant interactions, and the production build. For math typography, verify that the KaTeX stylesheet and its font assets load in development and in the built site; inspect representative inline and display formulas in the browser for the intended KaTeX glyphs and spacing. A successful TeX render or build alone does not prove that the fonts loaded. Save findings against the reviewed source revision. Existing test success is not evidence that every UI interaction or scholarly claim was checked.

Use the project's actual hosting integration and existing publication authorization. Report the delivered manuscript/site and any unsupported feature accurately. Creating this skill or a format document alone is not a publication request.

Ownership

The generic specification, examples, and note-writing workflows belong to this skill. Consumers link to that canonical material; project adapters, manuscript registries, scholarly content, implementation mappings, and review records belong to the project. Editing a manuscript generated from an example is ordinary authoring; maintaining another writable copy of the generic specification or template is not.

When the specification changes, update its version and record compatibility changes. Projects declare their adopted version and migrate deliberately. Preserve user instructions and project publication scope.
